passages.original: Caeterum non ignoro, Pammachi charissime, a multis Ecclesiasticis praetermissam : et qui exponere sunt conati, apud Graecos reperi Apollinarem Laodicenum, qui cum in adolescentia sua breves et in hunc et in alios prophetas com- menta(??)olos reliquisset, tangens magis sensus, quam explicans, rogatus est postea, ut in Osee. plenius scriberet : qui liber venit in nostras manus; sed et ipse nimia brevitate ad perfectam intelligentiam lectorem docere non potest. Origenes parvum de hoc propheta scripsit libellum, cui hunc titulum imposuit, περί τσΰ πώς ώ'ομάιθ/] fey τω Έφραίμ, hoc est, quare appellatur in Osee Ephraim volens ostendere quaecunque contra eum dicuntur, ad haereticorum referenda personam.
passages.english: But I am not unaware, dearest Pammachius, that [this prophet] has been passed over by many churchmen; and of those who have tried to expound [him], I found among the Greeks Apollinaris of Laodicea, who, after he had in his youth left brief little commentaries both on this and on other prophets, touching on the meanings rather than explaining them, was afterwards asked to write more fully on Hosea; that book has come into our hands, but it too, through excessive brevity, cannot bring the reader to a complete understanding. Origen wrote a small booklet on this prophet, to which he gave this title: "On why Ephraim is so named in Hosea," that is, why Ephraim is so called in Hosea, wishing to show that whatever is said against him is to be applied to the person of the heretics.
passages.notes: "com- menta(??)olos" is garbled; read as commentariolos (little commentaries). The Greek title is badly scanned; it appears to be περὶ τοῦ πῶς ὠνομάσθη ἐν τῷ Ὠσηὲ Ἐφραίμ, matching Jerome's Latin gloss. The object of "praetermissam" (feminine) is not expressed in this passage; presumably the prophecy of Hosea.

passages.original: ut pariter audire et nosse valeamus quid vaticinetur Osee propheta, in cujus explanationem secundum dictabimus [Al. dicta- mus] librum. Cumque tuo laeter adminiculo, et in prima urbe terrarum, primum et nobilitato et re- ligione habere mo gaudeam defensorem, tamen magis optarem illud inibi contingere, quod Titus Livius scribit de Catone, cujus gloriae neque pro- fuit quisquam laudando, nec vituperando no- cuit 3, cum utrumque summis praediti fecerint ingeniis. Significat autem M Ciceronem et C. Cae- sarem, quorum alter laudes, alter vituperationes supradicti scripsit viri. Dum enim vivimus et in vase fragili continemur, videntur amico- rum prodesse studia, et nocere aemulorum opprobria.
passages.english: so that we may alike hear and know what the prophet Hosea prophesies, in explanation of whom we shall dictate the second book. And although I rejoice in your support, and am glad to have in the first city of the world a defender first both in nobility and in religion, yet I would rather that the same thing happen to me there that Titus Livy writes of Cato: that no one helped his glory by praising, nor harmed it by censuring, though both were done by men endowed with the highest talents. He means Marcus Cicero and Gaius Caesar, one of whom wrote praises, the other censures, of the aforementioned man. For while we live and are contained in a fragile vessel, the efforts of friends seem to help us, and the reproaches of rivals to harm us.
passages.notes: "Al. dictamus" is a variant reading ("we are dictating"). "mo" read as "me". Stray numeral "3" after nocuit is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Et de haere- ticis quidem non est dubium, quin de domo 103 Dei ejecti sint, et non addat ut diligat eos, quan- diu in errore permanserint, omnesque principes eorum recedentes a Deo sunt, sive inobedientes, ut Valentinus, Marcion, ct caeteri. Possumus principes haereticorum daemones dicere, qui vere a Deo re- cesserunt, et appellantur principes, juxta quod Do- minus loquitur in Evangelio : Veniet3princeps hujus mundi, et inveniet in me nihil (Joan.XIV, 30). Et Apostolus adversus potestates, principatus ct rectores tenebrarum istarum pugnare nos dicit (Ephes.VI). Queritur autem juxta historiam, quo- modo de domo sua ejecerit eos, id est, decem tri- bus, cum in domo Dei non fuerint?
passages.english: And concerning the heretics there is indeed no doubt that they have been cast out of the house of God, and that he will not again love them so long as they remain in error, and that all their leaders are withdrawing from God, or disobedient, like Valentinus, Marcion, and the rest. We can call the demons the leaders of the heretics, who truly withdrew from God and are called princes, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel: "The prince of this world will come, and will find nothing in me" (John 14:30). And the Apostle says that we fight against powers, principalities and the rulers of this darkness (Ephesians 6). But it is asked, according to the historical sense, how he cast them, that is, the ten tribes, out of his house, when they were not in the house of God?
passages.notes: "103" is a page number and "3" after "Veniet" a footnote mark; both omitted. "principes" is rendered "leaders" for the heretics and "princes" for the demons, to keep the link with "princeps hujus mundi" ("prince of this world") in the Gospel quotation. "Queritur" is read as "Quaeritur".
